# Create Your First AI Image with Midjourney: A Beginner Walkthrough

> **In short:** Midjourney turns a written description into a picture in roughly a minute. You'll need a Midjourney subscription (no free tier), about ten minutes, and a clear idea of what you want. The finished image is yours to download and use.

In the next ten minutes, you'll go from a blank screen to a finished picture saved on your device. No art background needed — if you can describe what you want to see, you can do this. We'll skip the jargon and focus on the buttons you'll actually press.

## Before you start

- **A Midjourney account** — sign up on the official Midjourney website. A paid subscription is required; Midjourney does not currently offer a permanent free tier.
- **A Discord account (optional)** — Midjourney also runs inside Discord, the chat app. Either path works; this guide uses the website because it's the simplest for first-timers.
- **About 10–15 minutes** of your time, plus another minute or so while the AI draws.
- **One clear idea** of a picture you'd like to see. "A cat" works as a starter; "a calico cat asleep on a stack of books, soft morning light" gives a much better result.

## Step 1 — Create your Midjourney account

Open your web browser and go to the Midjourney homepage. Look for a button like **"Sign In"** or **"Get Started"** in the top-right corner. Click it, then sign in with your email, a Google account, or a Discord login.

You'll land on a screen asking you to choose a subscription plan. Pick the cheapest one if this is a first try — you can upgrade later if you like the tool. After you confirm payment, the page reloads and drops you into your personal Midjourney workspace, with a left-hand sidebar.

If you started in Discord instead, the same tool runs inside a chat window. Either path leads to the same picture-quality results.

You'll know it worked when you see a sidebar with options like **"Imagine"** or **"Create,"** and your username in a corner.

## Step 2 — Open the create screen

From the sidebar, look for an entry labeled something like **"Imagine"**, **"Create"**, or a small **+** icon. Click it. A new panel opens with an empty text box — usually wide, sitting near the top — and a faint placeholder phrase such as *"Imagine…"* or *"/imagine"*.

This box is where you'll describe your picture. Think of it as one blank sentence waiting to be filled in. Don't type yet — just confirm the cursor is inside the box and the rest of the screen looks like a clean, mostly empty workspace.

If your version looks like a Discord chat instead, type the slash command **/imagine** in any chat field. Discord will autocomplete it for you.

You'll know it worked when your cursor is blinking inside the text box and no error message is showing.

## Step 3 — Write your first prompt

In the text box, describe one picture in plain words. Imagine texting a friend who paints for you — tell them the subject, the mood, the setting, and the style. A **prompt** is just the name for this description; nothing fancy.

Be specific. *"A flower"* gives you a generic flower. *"A single red poppy in a glass jar, morning sunlight, photo-realistic"* gives you something that actually looks the way you pictured it. Short sentences are fine. So is a comma-separated list.

When your description feels right, look for a small button nearby — usually a paper-plane icon, an arrow, or the word **"Generate"** — and click it once. Don't click twice; every click spends a credit and starts a fresh image.

💬 Example: `a cozy reading nook by a window, warm lamp light, watercolor illustration, soft colors`

You'll know it worked when the button greys out, a small progress message appears, and within about a minute the first signs of your picture start forming on screen.

## Step 4 — Read the image grid

When generation finishes, you'll see a **2×2 grid** of four images — four different attempts at your prompt. They're all based on the same description, but each one took the words a slightly different way.

Look at all four. Which one feels closest to what you imagined? Which has a color, angle, or detail you really like? You don't have to pick yet — for now, just notice that the four pictures are different from each other, even though you only typed one prompt.

If none of the four feels right, look for a button like **"Re-roll"** or a circular **↻** arrow near the grid. That tells Midjourney to try again with the same prompt and produce four new attempts.

You'll know it worked when you can clearly see four distinct images and at least one of them makes you think *"ooh, that's nice."*

## Step 5 — Upscale your favorite

Below or beside the grid, you'll find a row of small buttons. The pattern is usually **U1, U2, U3, U4** — one under each image — for **upscaling**, which means turning the small preview into a full-size, sharp picture. There are also **V1–V4** buttons, which create **variations** on that specific image.

Click the **U** button under the picture you like most. Within a few seconds, a single full-resolution version of that image appears. This is the one you'll keep.

If the upscaled image has a small detail you'd like changed — say the cat's eyes are the wrong color — you can run a new variation on it, or simply upscale a different image from the grid.

You'll know it worked when a single, larger, sharper image replaces or appears next to the small grid preview.

## Step 6 — Download the image to your device

Click the upscaled image to open it full-size. Look for a **download icon** (usually a downward arrow ⬇), or a button labeled **"Open in Browser"** or **"Save"**. One click downloads a PNG or JPG file straight to your device.

On a phone, the image often opens in a new tab — press and hold it, then choose **"Save to Photos"** or **"Download"** from the menu that pops up. On a computer, it lands in your Downloads folder.

The file is now yours. You can post it, print it, set it as your wallpaper, or send it to a friend. Paid-plan downloads carry no watermark.

You'll know it worked when the file appears in your **Downloads** folder (computer) or **Photos / Gallery** app (phone), and you can open it again from there.

## Common mistakes

- **Writing a one-word prompt.** "Cat" gives you a random cat. Always include at least one detail about mood, style, or setting — Step 3 has an example you can copy.
- **Clicking Generate twice in a hurry.** Once is enough. Every extra click spends a credit and starts a fresh image. If the first result isn't ready yet, just wait — a progress indicator is showing.
- **Asking the AI to draw readable text.** Midjourney struggles with words inside images — a sign that says "OPEN" often comes out misspelled. Use a real text tool or a graphic editor for readable words, and let Midjourney handle the rest.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** your first image is great for a phone wallpaper, a birthday card, or a custom avatar — small personal touches that feel one-of-a-kind without costing a designer's fee.
- **For your business or work:** a single Midjourney picture can become a blog header, a slide background, or a quick mockup for a client conversation. It's not a replacement for a designer on real projects, but it's a fast way to test an idea visually.
- **If you're just getting started:** the easiest first move is to re-run the same prompt with one word changed each time — *"watercolor"* becomes *"oil painting"* becomes *"pencil sketch"* — and watch how the style shifts while the subject stays the same.

## Try it now

Take one minute and write down a single sentence describing a picture you actually want to see. Then open Midjourney, paste it into the Imagine box, and hit Generate. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, your first image will probably be ready to look at.
